title: The Waggon Train to the Great Cipher: Bazeries and the Reading of What Was Not Meant to Be Read
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Port and the Volunteer of the Train

stops.name: Port-Vendres, birth in the garrison port
stops.date_confidence: attested; en.wikipedia and fr.wikipedia independently give 21 August 1846 at Port-Vendres, and the commemorative plaque in the town repeats both
stops.campa: The Mediterranean cuts into the Roussillon coast at Port-Vendres, a fishing harbour and garrison anchorage a few miles short of the Spanish border, and on the twenty-first of August a son is born there to a family of the town. They name him Étienne. The quays load troops and mail for Algeria; the business of the place is departure. No schooling of any distinction is ever recorded for him. Nothing in the register marks the child for anything beyond the ordinary trades of the coast: the boats, the customs house, the Algerian run.
suggested_refs: The monument aux morts of Port-Vendres, which carries his commemorative plaque

stops.name: Port-Vendres, the volunteer of the Fourth Squadron
stops.date_confidence: date attested to the day by the Légion d'honneur service record (Léonore LH//150/51, matricule 68), which enters entry into service at the 4e Escadron du Train des Équipages Militaires as engagé volontaire, soldat de 2e classe, 26 August 1863; the same record gives Port-Vendres only as family domicile and names no enlistment town, and the squadron depot lay elsewhere, so this pin is a domicile proxy and not an attested place of enlistment
stops.campa: Five days after his seventeenth birthday he signs on for seven years, volunteer of the second class in the Fourth Squadron of the Train des Équipages Militaires. It is the supply arm: waggons, mules, forage, the least regarded corner of the French army. He enters at the bottom of it. There is no academy behind him, no Polytechnique and no Saint-Cyr, and the staff officers whose ciphers he will one day take apart in front of witnesses have all passed through one. The clerk enters the date, the squadron, and the boy's height.
suggested_refs: Léonore LH//150/51, the Légion d'honneur dossier, matricule 68, whose service column runs from 1863 to 1899

segments.name: Metz, the Capitulation, and the Rank Taken Back

stops.name: Metz, the commission of the twenty-third of October
stops.date_confidence: attested as to date by Léonore LH//150/51, which enters sous-lieutenant, 23 October 1870, and re-enters the same date lower on the sheet; en.wikipedia's 13 October 1870 is wrong by ten days. The record names no place, and Metz here follows the dossier's unverified attribution of Bazeries to the 2nd Corps of the Army of the Rhine
stops.campa: The Army of the Rhine is shut inside Metz with Bazaine, sortie after sortie thrown at the Prussian ring and beaten back, the train's own horses going into the pot. On the twenty-third of October, four days before the capitulation, the supply sergeant is made sous-lieutenant. The service sheet enters the promotion twice and writes no place beside it either time. Seven years in the ranks have bought him the rank four days before the army conferring it ceases to exist. Inside the walls the ration is horsemeat and the last of the flour.
suggested_refs: The siege of Metz, 19 August to 27 October 1870, and Bazaine's Army of the Rhine
sources: en.wikipedia.org, 'Étienne Bazeries' (military career section, with the ten-day discrepancy)

stops.name: Metz, the largest capitulation in French history
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the capitulation date is general history, but Bazeries's presence at Metz and his attachment to the 2nd Corps come from the dossier's reading of the Légion d'honneur file and could not be confirmed against an independently fetched source in this pass
stops.campa: Bazaine surrenders Metz and its garrison on the twenty-seventh, some hundred and seventy thousand men marched off into Germany without a battle, the capitulation France will spend a generation refusing to forgive. The new sous-lieutenant goes with them. Nothing he has learned about waggons and forage applies to a column of prisoners walking east under guard. Which corps he was serving with when the gates opened, and by what road he was taken out, the accessible record does not settle.
suggested_refs: The Prussian prisoner convoys out of Metz, October and November 1870
sources: Dossier attribution to LH//150/51, unverified this session

stops.name: Near the Metz lines, out in a mason's clothes
stops.date_confidence: the escape and the disguise are attested by en.wikipedia ('captured but escaped disguised as a bricklayer'); the month and the site are inferred from the capitulation date and are not recorded anywhere reached
stops.campa: He gets out. The encyclopaedias give the method in six words and no more: captured, escaped, disguised as a bricklayer. Somewhere between the prisoner columns and the French lines a supply officer puts on a mason's clothes, carries a mason's tools, and walks past guards who are looking for soldiers. It is the first thing in his file he does by reading a system rather than obeying it. Nothing else about it is written down anywhere reached in this research: not the date, not the road, not whether anyone went with him.
suggested_refs: Escape narratives of French officers from the Metz convoys, autumn 1870

stops.name: Orléans, the improvised army of the Loire
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, dossier only; no source fetched this session places Bazeries in the Loire campaign, and the claim is carried here because deleting it would hide a gap rather than close it
stops.campa: South of Paris, Gambetta and Freycinet raise new armies out of nothing to break the ring around the capital, and Bazeries is said to have served in that improvised campaign along the Loire through the winter. The Army of the Loire wins at Coulmiers and is broken at Orléans, veterans of Metz fighting beside conscripts who have never held a rifle. He is nowhere named in any account of it that could be reached in this research. The claim rests on the dossier and on nothing else.
suggested_refs: The Army of the Loire, November 1870 to January 1871, and the second battle of Orléans
sources: Dossier only; not corroborated by any independently fetched source

stops.name: Lyon, forty-eight hours of interior duty
stops.date_confidence: attested by the campaigns block of Léonore LH//150/51, which reads: à l'Intérieur, Lyon, du 30 Avril 1871 au 1er Mai 1871. The dossier's fortnight-long posting and its Commune framing are both wrong and are corrected here
stops.campa: On the thirtieth of April the service record puts him at Lyon, interior duty, and on the first of May it takes him away again. Two days. The tradition that stretched these two days into a fortnight and hung the Commune on them fails on the calendar: the killing in Paris comes three weeks after he has gone. The campaigns column of a French officer's file counts such things scrupulously, and forty-eight hours at Lyon is the whole of what it counts here. In January he had been made lieutenant en second, a field promotion of the collapse, and he is wearing it.
suggested_refs: The campaigns column of Léonore LH//150/51, which records two African tours and this single interior posting

stops.name: Paris, the commission of review takes the lieutenancy back
stops.date_confidence: attested by Léonore LH//150/51: remis Sous-Lieutenant par décision du 29 février 1872 de la commission instituée par la loi du 10 Août 1871. The record does not say where Bazeries himself was; the pin is the canonical Paris pin, where the commission constituted by that law sat, not an attested location for the man
stops.campa: The law of the tenth of August 1871 sets up a commission to review the ranks handed out during the collapse, and the commission works its way down the lists. On the twenty-ninth of February 1872 it reaches Bazeries and takes back his lieutenancy: remis sous-lieutenant, the sheet says, returned to the lower grade by decision of the commission. The record does not say where he was standing when it happened, or whether anyone told him in person. He earns the rank a second time in the ordinary way, by waiting, and is confirmed lieutenant on the twenty-sixth of April 1874.
suggested_refs: The law of 10 August 1871 and its commission of revision of wartime commissions

segments.name: Africa, Châteauroux, and the Captain's Stripes

stops.name: Algiers, the first African tour
stops.date_confidence: the tour is attested to the day by the campaigns block of Léonore LH//150/51 (en Afrique du 8 Mai 1875 au 9 Février 1876), and the year by both language editions of Wikipedia; Algiers itself is an unconfirmed staging proxy, since the file names no Algerian garrison. Coordinates snapped to the standard Algiers centroid
stops.campa: On the eighth of May he sails for Africa, a lieutenant of the train on his first colonial tour, and the file closes the tour on the ninth of February the following year. Where in Algeria he served it does not say. The train followed the columns inland, hauling water and cartridges over ground the maps barely covered, and the arm that fed a campaign learned what a campaign actually was. He lands back in France on the ninth of February 1876 and is posted to the Third Company of the Ninth Squadron the following day.
suggested_refs: The train des équipages in the Algerian interior columns of the 1870s

stops.name: Châteauroux, the marriage of the twenty-sixth of April
stops.date_confidence: attested; the état civil block of Léonore LH//150/51 reads marié le 26 Avril 1876 à demoiselle Marie Louise Élodie Berthon, alors domiciliée à Châteauroux, département de l'Indre, with the ministerial marriage authorisation noted as of 1 August 1876. This corrects the dossier's placement of the wedding in Roussillon, roughly seven hundred kilometres away
stops.campa: He marries in the Indre, far inland from the sea he was born beside. The tradition that set this wedding near his birthplace on the Mediterranean is wrong by some seven hundred kilometres: the service sheet names Châteauroux, and the bride, Marie-Louise-Élodie Berthon, is domiciled there. Ten weeks earlier he had been in Algeria. The ministerial authorisation an officer needed before he could marry follows on the first of August, fourteen weeks after the wedding it was meant to permit.
suggested_refs: The état civil block of Léonore LH//150/51, naming the bride's domicile
sources: en.wikipedia.org, 'Étienne Bazeries' (marriage and spouse, no location given)

stops.name: Châteauroux, captain, and detached to the artillery
stops.date_confidence: the captaincy of 12 January 1877 is given in Wikipedia's career timeline; the same-day detachment to the artillery direction at Châteauroux, and a second detachment on 9 February 1877, are entered in the service column of Léonore LH//150/51
stops.campa: On the twelfth of January he is made captain and detached to the artillery direction at Châteauroux, his wife's town, and detached there a second time in February. He is thirty years old and has been in uniform for thirteen years, all of them spent moving other men's supplies. Artillery is not his arm. It is the first time his service puts him near the technical branches, where instruments are made and tables are computed. What a train officer was doing inside an artillery establishment, the file does not explain.
suggested_refs: The direction d'artillerie of Châteauroux and its manufacturing establishment

stops.name: Constantine, four years of Africa without a place-name
stops.date_confidence: the tour is attested by the campaigns block of Léonore LH//150/51 (en Afrique du 18 Mai 1878 au 6 Juin 1882), which corrects the dossier's start date of 19 March 1878 by two months while confirming the end date exactly; Constantine is an acknowledged guess, since the file names no Algerian town, and the dossier's credit of five campaigns is not supported by a record listing two African tours in all
stops.campa: The eighteenth of May opens his second African tour, and it runs four years and nineteen days, to the sixth of June 1882. Four years of a man's life sit under a place-name nobody can confirm: Constantine is a guess, a plausible one, hung on a gorge city that held a garrison, and the file names no Algerian town anywhere. What the file gives instead is units and dates, the Twelfth Squadron of the train from April 1878, the Third Company of the Eleventh from April 1882, and the day he came home.
suggested_refs: The campaigns block of Léonore LH//150/51, listing two African tours and no garrison towns
sources: Dossier claim of a Constantine posting, unverified

stops.name: Paris, chevalier of the Légion d'honneur
stops.date_confidence: attested by en.wikipedia, which dates the decree 28 December 1888 and gives his grade at the time as captain in the train arm; the pin is the canonical Paris pin for the decree, not an attested location for Bazeries on that day
stops.campa: A decree of the twenty-eighth of December makes Captain Bazeries of the train des équipages a chevalier of the Légion d'honneur. He is forty-two. Twenty-five years of service stand behind the cross and not one line of cryptography: no book, no device, no solved dispatch, nothing that would tell a reader of the decree why this particular supply captain should ever be remembered. The citation names the arm, the rank, and the years, and it names nothing else.
suggested_refs: The Légion d'honneur decree of 28 December 1888, recorded in Léonore LH//150/51

segments.name: Nantes: Reading What Could Not Be Read

stops.name: Nantes, the army's own cipher read without the key
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to year and to General Fay's role, both of which come from bibmath and the dossier; the underlying fact that Bazeries solved messages in the official French military transposition system is attested by en.wikipedia. Month and day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: Stationed at Nantes with the Eleventh Corps, Bazeries tells the staff that the army's official transposition cipher can be read without the key, and General Fay puts the claim to the test. He reads it. The staff strengthens the system, and he reads the strengthened version too, before it ever reaches the units in the field. Seven years earlier Auguste Kerckhoffs had told this same army, in its own Journal des sciences militaires, that a cipher must go on holding even when the enemy knows the machine that made it.
suggested_refs: Auguste Kerckhoffs, 'La cryptographie militaire', Journal des sciences militaires, January and February 1883
sources: auguste_kerckhoffs.journey.json, stop 'Paris, 62 rue Claude-Bernard: the six desiderata'

stops.name: Nantes, Gendron's bundle of dead numbers
stops.date_confidence: contradiction flagged and left standing: bibmath's masquedefer page and en.wikipedia's 'Man in the Iron Mask' both date Gendron's handover to 1890, and only 1890 makes the roughly three years of work reach the 1893 publication; cryptiana's bazeries2.htm instead places the episode at Nantes in 1891. Month defaulted to 06 as an ordering device only
stops.campa: Commandant Louis Gendron, sifting seventeenth-century military correspondence, comes on sheets of numbers nobody has read since Louis XIV's clerks wrote them: dispatches to and from Marshal Catinat in Piedmont, locked in the cipher the Rossignol family built for the king. He hands the bundle to Bazeries. The sources disagree about the year and about the town, bibmath and the English encyclopaedia putting the handover in 1890 and cryptiana placing it at Nantes in 1891, and the disagreement cannot be settled from here. Three years of evenings begin.
suggested_refs: The ciphered correspondence of Louvois and Louis XIV with Marshal Nicolas de Catinat, Piedmont campaigns

stops.name: Nantes, the challenges of the inventor Bord
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, dossier only; the name Bord appears in no source fetched in this research, and the January 1891 dates are the dossier's alone
stops.campa: A Nantes inventor named Bord builds a printing cryptograph and sends Bazeries a cryptogram made on it. Bazeries reads it. The dossier alone reports this, and the name Bord appears in no independent source reached in this research. What it reports is that Bord sent a harder one, and then a harder one after that, through most of January, and that each came back read, the challenge issued in public and the answer handed back in front of the man who had issued it.
suggested_refs: Printing cryptograph devices of the French provincial inventors, 1880s and 1890s
sources: Dossier only; not corroborated by any independently fetched source

stops.name: Paris, the Ministry of War and the twenty disks
stops.date_confidence: the device is attested for 1891 by cryptomuseum's M-94 page (twenty discs, scrambled alphabets of twenty-five letters each); the precise date of 12 February and the submission to the Ministry of War are reconstruction, since the cited source says nothing of either. Édouard Lucas presented the device to the twentieth AFAS congress at Marseille on 19 September 1891, but no source places Bazeries himself in Marseille, so that presentation is cited here rather than staged as his stop
stops.campa: He brings the ministry a cylinder: twenty removable disks on a common axis, each carrying its own scrambled alphabet of twenty-five letters, the message set up along one line of the drum and read off along another. It is a good device. It is also, without his knowing it, a rediscovery, since Thomas Jefferson had described the same machine in 1795 and left the description among his papers, unread, for more than a century. The French army will not adopt it. The Americans will adopt its descendant thirty years later, and call it the M-94.
suggested_refs: Édouard Lucas, 'Cryptographe à 20 rondelles-alphabets', presented to the twentieth congress of the Association française pour l'avancement des sciences, Marseille, 19 September 1891
The U.S. Army M-94, conceived by Parker Hitt and developed by Joseph Mauborgne in 1917, adopted 1921 or 1922 depending on the source

segments.name: The Quai d'Orsay and the Cipher of the Sun King

stops.name: Quai d'Orsay, lent to the Bureau du Chiffre
stops.date_confidence: attested by en.wikipedia (1891, began working for the Foreign Ministry's cipher bureau) and by bibmath, which names the Bureau du Chiffre du ministère des affaires étrangères; the month of August comes from the dossier's chronology, and the day is defaulted to 01
stops.campa: The army lends him to the Foreign Ministry's Bureau du Chiffre, and the loan becomes the second half of his life. The Quai d'Orsay reads other governments' telegrams as a matter of routine and needs men who can do what Bazeries does without being asked to explain how. He is a train officer among diplomats, a man with no foreign languages working on messages written in languages he does not have. Christopher Andrew, going through the ministry's own papers long afterward, will call him un singulier bohème.
suggested_refs: Christopher Andrew, 'Codebreakers and Foreign Offices', in The Missing Dimension (Macmillan, 1984), on the Quai d'Orsay cipher bureau
sources: Andrew, The Missing Dimension (not fetched this session; carried as attributed tradition)

stops.name: Paris, the anarchists' polyalphabet and the squadron command
stops.date_confidence: the promotion to chef d'escadron on 10 July 1892 is reconstruction, given in the dossier's chronology and consistent with but not confirmed by Wikipedia's rank outline; the anarchist Gronsfeld solution and Bazeries's own high estimate of it come from the dossier's 1892 section and were not independently confirmed
stops.campa: He is made chef d'escadron in July, the rank that fixes him in every later account as Commandant Bazeries. The prefecture hands him anarchist correspondence in a decade when anarchists are leaving bombs in Paris cafés and police stations, and the cipher is a polyalphabetic of the Gronsfeld kind, from the family that has carried Blaise de Vigenère's name for three centuries. He reads it, and afterwards rates it the best solution of his life, ahead of the Great Cipher. Why he ranked it so high he never sets down.
suggested_refs: The anarchist bombing campaign in Paris, 1892 to 1894, and the police cipher work it generated
sources: en.wikipedia.org, 'Étienne Bazeries' (rank progression, without this date)

stops.name: Paris, les ennemis in five groups
stops.date_confidence: attested; bibmath's masquedefer page and both cryptiana pages independently give the syllabic insight, the reading of 124-22-125-46-345 as les-en-ne-mi-s, and the recovered nomenclator of 587 values. The year 1893 is the year of the resulting publication; month and day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: The Great Cipher has held for two hundred years because everyone attacking it assumed the numbers stood for letters, or at most for pairs of letters. Bazeries assumes syllables. He guesses that one recurring run in a military dispatch spells les ennemis, tries 124-22-125-46-345 as les-en-ne-mi-s, and the guess holds, and then holds again, and the whole nomenclator opens: five hundred and eighty-seven values, a syllabary with traps laid in it, the private speech of Louis XIV's war ministry.
suggested_refs: The Rossignol Grand Chiffre and its 587-value nomenclator as reconstructed by Bazeries

stops.name: Paris, Firmin-Didot prints Le Masque de fer
stops.date_confidence: the book and its 1893 Firmin-Didot imprint are attested (bribes.org, bibmath); the month is an ordering device only. The identification of Bulonde as the masked prisoner is Bazeries's own argument and is contested: Bulonde's arrest was publicised at the time, he was released by royal order on 11 December 1691, and his death is recorded in 1709, six years after the masked prisoner died on 19 November 1703. fr.wikipedia further notes recent analysis reading group 330 as gardien rather than masque, which would dissolve the identification entirely
stops.campa: With Émile Burgaud he publishes the decrypts as a book, and the book makes one claim that swallows all the others. In a dispatch of Louvois about General de Bulonde, who lifted the siege of Coni against orders, two groups stand where a word should be: 330 309. Bazeries reads them as masque. From that reading he names Bulonde as the man in the iron mask, and the identification runs through popular literature for a century afterward. Bulonde was released by royal order in December 1691 and died in 1709, six years after the masked prisoner.
stops.quote: Il n'est pas necessaire que je vous explique avec quel deplaisir Sa Majeste a appris le desordre avec lequel contre votre ordre et sans necessite Monsieur de Bulonde a pris le parti de lever le siege de Coni puisque Sa Majeste en connaissant mieux que personne les consequences connait aussi combien est grand le prejudice que l'on recevra de n'avoir pas pris cette place dont il faudra tacher de se rendre maitre pendant l'hiver. Elle desire que vous fassiez arreter Monsieur de Bulonde et le fassiez conduire a la citadelle de Pignerol ou Sa Majeste veut qu'il soit garde enferme pendant la nuit dans une chambre de ladite citadelle et le jour ayant la liberte de se promener sur les remparts avec un 330 309.
stops.quote_source: Bazeries's decryption of the Louvois dispatch, in Émile Burgaud and Commandant Bazeries, Le Masque de fer: Révélation de la correspondance chiffrée de Louis XIV (Paris: Firmin-Didot, 1893), as transcribed in the fr.wikipedia article 'Homme au masque de fer'
suggested_refs: David Kahn, 'The Man in the Iron Mask, Encore et Enfin, Cryptologically', Cryptologia 29, no. 1 (January 2005), 43-49, reprinted in How I Discovered World War II's Greatest Spy (2014), 421-426, rejecting the Bulonde reading

stops.name: Paris, A. Hermann prints the Tables chiffrantes
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the title and the A. Hermann imprint come from the dossier's citation, unconfirmed by any catalogue reached this session, and the publisher's Left Bank address is traditional rather than verified. Month is an ordering device
stops.campa: The Paris house of A. Hermann prints his Tables chiffrantes et déchiffrantes, ou Chiffre Bazeries, a working system offered to the army that has just declined his cylinder. He is publishing in two registers at once: the antiquarian, reading dead kings' mail, and the practical, telling the general staff how it ought to be encrypting its own. The bibliographic record for this one is thin. No catalogue reached in this research confirms the imprint, and the publisher's Left Bank address is traditional rather than verified.
suggested_refs: A. Hermann, Left Bank scientific publisher, catalogue of the 1890s
sources: Dossier citation only; not independently confirmed

stops.name: Constantine, the third African command
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, dossier only; the third African tour of 30 January to 3 July 1894 and the command of the train at Constantine appear in no source fetched this session, and Constantine is unrepresented in any other traveller's file checked. Month defaulted for ordering
stops.campa: He goes back to Africa a third time, in command of the train at Constantine, and comes home on the third of July 1894. No independent source reached in this research mentions the posting; the dossier alone attests it. Between the Great Cipher and the affair about to break in Paris, at the exact moment his name is becoming known, he spends half a year on a garrison in the Algerian interior doing the work he was commissioned to do at seventeen: waggons, forage, water hauled over ground the maps barely cover.
suggested_refs: The train des équipages at Constantine, 1893 to 1894
sources: Dossier only; not corroborated this session

segments.name: The Affair and the Bureau That Got It Wrong

stops.name: Quai d'Orsay, recalled to the Minister's disposal
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the specific date of 29 September 1894 is the dossier's alone, though a Foreign Ministry attachment in this period is plausible given the confirmed 1891 attachment. Dreyfus's arrest at the Ministry of War on 15 October 1894 is attested on his own file
stops.campa: On the twenty-ninth of September the army again places him at the disposal of the Minister of Foreign Affairs. The date of the recall is the dossier's, and nothing fetched in this research confirms it. Sixteen days later Alfred Dreyfus is arrested at the Ministry of War on the strength of a torn note taken from a wastebasket, and within six weeks the Bureau du Chiffre he has just rejoined is handling the one intercepted telegram capable of ending the case in the accused man's favour.
suggested_refs: The bordereau of the wastebasket and the arrest of 15 October 1894
sources: captain_alfred_dreyfus.journey.json, stop 'Paris, the arrest at the Ministry of War'

stops.name: Quai d'Orsay, the Panizzardi telegram
stops.date_confidence: the telegram's send date of 2 November 1894 and the decryption sequence are attested by bibmath's dedicated page: a fragmentary and incriminating reading around 6 November, the complete and exonerating text by 13 November. The dossier's 10 November is wrong. Bazeries's personal participation is unresolved and contested: Kahn found no record proving it, Andrew attributes the faulty ending to him, and neither bibmath nor fr.wikipedia's article on the telegram names him at all, crediting only the Quai d'Orsay cipher team. fr.wikipedia further attributes the false version circulated to the Cour de cassation to Hubert Henry, reconstructing it from memory in 1898
stops.campa: On the second of November the Italian military attaché Panizzardi telegraphs Rome in cipher about the arrested captain. Around the sixth the bureau has a fragment that can be read as damning. By the thirteenth it has the whole of it, and the whole of it says the opposite: se capitano Dreyfus non ha avuto relazione costa, if Captain Dreyfus has had no dealings with you. Which hands did which part of that work is not settled. Kahn found no record placing Bazeries on the telegram, Andrew lays the bad ending at his door, and the French sources name nobody.
suggested_refs: fr.wikipedia, 'Télégramme de Panizzardi', which credits the decryption to the Quai d'Orsay cipher team without naming an individual
David Kahn, The Codebreakers (Scribner, 1996), on the absence of evidence for Bazeries's participation
sources: bibmath.net, page on the Panizzardi telegram

stops.name: Fontainebleau, the emperor's weak field ciphers
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, dossier only; the fifty-seven page study of Napoleon's Hamburg-campaign ciphers and its serialisation in L'Abeille de Fontainebleau could not be located in any catalogue reached this session
stops.campa: He publishes fifty-seven pages on the ciphers Napoleon's staff used in the Hamburg campaign of 1813, first in the local paper at Fontainebleau, an unlikely place to print a cryptologic monograph. The verdict is that the emperor's field ciphers were weak and that his enemies read them without much trouble. It is the same charge he has been making against the living general staff, laid this time on a dead one, where no serving officer's career is at stake. The publication is dossier-only and remains unlocated.
suggested_refs: L'Abeille de Fontainebleau, September 1896, serialisation of the study of the 1813 ciphers
sources: Dossier only; not located on BnF, Gallica, or any catalogue fetched

stops.name: Paris, the Fashoda decrypt that went wrong
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the 30 September 1898 misreading, the portrait of Bazeries as poorly educated, without languages, alcoholic and a compulsive gambler, and the attribution to him of faulty Foreign Ministry decrypts all come from Christopher Andrew's essay in The Missing Dimension (1984), which could not be fetched or confirmed in this research
stops.campa: Marchand's column and Kitchener's have met on the upper Nile and two empires are within a step of war over a mud fort. On the thirtieth of September a decrypt goes wrong at the Quai d'Orsay, and Christopher Andrew, working through the ministry's papers eighty years later, lays it at Bazeries's door along with the bad ending of the Panizzardi telegram. Andrew's Bazeries drinks, gambles, has no languages and no education, and is brilliant and unreliable in the same week. That portrait rests on archives this research could not open.
suggested_refs: Christopher Andrew, 'Codebreakers and Foreign Offices', in The Missing Dimension (Macmillan, 1984)
sources: Dossier attribution to Andrew (1984); not independently fetched

stops.name: Paris, the Orléanist letters and the High Court
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, dossier only; the Chevilly traffic, the decoded reply from Philippe, Duke of Orléans, and the subsequent testimony before the Haute Cour de justice appear in no source fetched this session
stops.campa: The Orléanist partisans of the pretender Philippe are corresponding in cipher about a restoration. The traffic passing through Chevilly comes to Bazeries, and he opens it, including a short reply in the pretender's own hand. No source fetched in this research mentions any of this, and the dossier carries the episode alone. The High Court hears him afterward on what the letters say. What the pretender's reply actually contained, the dossier does not report.
suggested_refs: The 1899 Haute Cour de justice proceedings against the nationalist and royalist conspirators
sources: Dossier only; not corroborated this session

segments.name: The Retirement That Was Not One

stops.name: Paris, out of the active army
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested by both Wikipedia editions (retired 1899, at about fifty-three); the exact date of 18 March and Paris as the place are dossier-only and were not confirmed by anything fetched this session
stops.campa: After thirty-five years he leaves the active army. He is fifty-two. The career that began with a seventeen-year-old signing on for waggon duty ends with a chef d'escadron whose actual employer, for the last eight years, has been the Foreign Ministry rather than the War Ministry. Nothing about the retirement changes what he does with his days, or where he does it, or who pays him for it. Only the year is corroborated; the date and the place come from the dossier.
suggested_refs: Léonore LH//150/51, whose service column closes in 1899
sources: Dossier chronology for the exact date

stops.name: Paris, the Ministry of War refuses the last cipher
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, dossier only; neither the proposal nor the rejection of 19 April 1899 appears in any source fetched this session
stops.campa: A month after leaving the service he offers the ministry a last hand cipher, pencil and paper, no apparatus at all, and the ministry declines it: not secure enough under heavy traffic. Neither the proposal nor the refusal appears in any source fetched in this research, and the dossier carries both alone. He has spent a decade telling the general staff that its ciphers were readable, and the staff has now said the same thing back to him about his. Whether he took that as vindication or as a door shut in his face, the record does not say.
suggested_refs: The Commission de cryptographie of the French Ministry of War, 1890s deliberations
sources: Dossier only; not corroborated this session

stops.name: Paris, Fasquelle prints Les Chiffres secrets dévoilés
stops.date_confidence: attested; the BnF catalogue and OpenLibrary record OL2914915M agree on E. Fasquelle, Paris, 1901, 282 pages, and apprendre-en-ligne confirms the same imprint. The dossier's Charpentier et Fasquelle reflects the Bibliothèque-Charpentier series rather than the imprint of record. Month and day defaulted to 01; the key phrases are cited by bribes.org to pages 204 to 205 of the book, transcribed there rather than read from the Gallica page image, which returned HTTP 403
stops.campa: Fasquelle publishes Les Chiffres secrets dévoilés, two hundred and eighty-two pages surveying cipher from antiquity to the general staff's present practice, with his own solutions set out as worked examples and the staff's habits attacked by name. Among the key phrases printed for the cylinder's mixed alphabets, between a line of the Marseillaise and a patriotic motto, sits one that is neither of those things. It is a soldier's marching song about fried onions, and he put it in a cipher book.
stops.quote_source: Étienne Bazeries, Les Chiffres secrets dévoilés (Paris: E. Fasquelle, 1901), 204-205, one of the fourteen key-phrases for the cylinder's mixed alphabets, transcribed at bribes.org/crypto/cryptographe_Bazeries.html
suggested_refs: Wikimedia Commons, Category: Étienne Bazeries, holding a full PDF scan of the 1901 book and a National Cryptologic Museum photograph of the cylinder illustration
Harvard University Library Microreproduction Department, 35mm microfilm of the 1901 edition, 1983

stops.name: Paris, the Japanese code he could not read
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the episode is drawn from Christopher Andrew's essay in The Missing Dimension (1984), which could not be fetched or confirmed in this research. Month and day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: The Russo-Japanese War opens and fragments of a Japanese diplomatic code reach the police. Bazeries works on them about a week and returns the verdict that the book cannot be reconstructed. A commissaire named Haverna and one assistant then reconstruct most of it inside two months. Andrew is the only source for the episode, and Andrew could not be opened in this research. Nothing records what Bazeries said about it afterward, or whether anyone thought to ask him.
suggested_refs: Christopher Andrew, 'Codebreakers and Foreign Offices', in The Missing Dimension (Macmillan, 1984), on Haverna and the Japanese codebook
sources: Dossier attribution to Andrew (1984); not independently fetched

stops.name: Versailles, the decipherer with no post
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, dossier only; the Versailles working arrangement appears in no source fetched this session, and the date is an ordering device covering a period the dossier gives loosely as roughly 1899 to the 1920s
stops.campa: Retired from the army and past sixty, he goes on working for the Foreign Ministry for pay, and a good deal of that work is done at Versailles rather than in Paris. Nothing fetched in this research corroborates the arrangement, which is recorded here as the dossier's claim. He is by then the state's decipherer the way a man becomes a fixture rather than an appointment: not established, not on any list, simply the one they send it to. It carries no title and appears in no organigram.
suggested_refs: The Quai d'Orsay's contract cryptanalysts of the pre-war decade
sources: Dossier only; not corroborated this session

stops.name: Paris, officier of the Légion d'honneur
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the decree date of 30 December 1907 is named in the dossier's chronology, and the Léonore notice that would confirm it returned only a search-page header rather than record content when called in this research
stops.campa: A decree of the thirtieth of December raises him officier of the Légion d'honneur, nineteen years after the chevalier's cross. The first cross went to a supply captain who had done nothing remarkable at all. This one is for the cylinder, the Great Cipher, the anarchists, the Orléanists, and a body of work inside the Bureau du Chiffre that the state has never described in public and never will. The Léonore notice that would put the date beyond doubt returned a search header and nothing else.
suggested_refs: Léonore, Archives nationales, notice 22690, the Bazeries dossier

segments.name: The Last War, Noyon, and the Plaque

stops.name: Paris, the German cryptograms of the war
stops.date_confidence: attested in general by en.wikipedia, which records that he worked on German codes during the First World War and that he did not head the wartime Section du Chiffre; the specific solutions, the dates, and his working location are not itemised in any source fetched this session, and the pin is the canonical Paris pin
stops.campa: He is sixty-seven when the war begins, and he goes back to work on German cryptograms. He does not head the Section du Chiffre. That is a younger service now, with men like Georges Painvin inside it, and the traffic is radio, thousands of intercepts a day, industrial in a way nothing in his career prepared him for. What exactly he solved is itemised nowhere that could be reached in this research. The only itemised claim stands on a plaque his birthplace raises later, and a plaque is not an archive.
suggested_refs: The French Section du Chiffre of 1914 to 1918 and the work of Georges Painvin on the ADFGVX cipher

stops.name: Paris, the last cryptogram at seventy-eight
stops.date_confidence: the retirement from cryptanalytic work in 1924, at seventy-eight, is attested by both Wikipedia editions and bibmath; where he was living by then is not recorded in anything fetched this session, and the Paris pin stands for the ministry that employed him rather than for a residence. Month and day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: He stops at seventy-eight. Sixty-one years after signing on as a volunteer of the second class, and twenty-five after his official retirement from the army, he puts down the work that was never quite a job. Where he was living by then is not recorded in anything reached in this research, and the pin here stands for the ministry that employed him rather than for a house he slept in. There is no ceremony recorded and no successor named, and nothing says a file was ever handed over.
suggested_refs: The Quai d'Orsay cipher service of the early 1920s

stops.name: Noyon, death in the rebuilt town
stops.date_confidence: attested; en.wikipedia and fr.wikipedia both give death at Noyon, Oise, on 7 November 1931, aged eighty-five. Why he was at Noyon is recorded nowhere reached
stops.campa: He dies at Noyon in the Oise on the seventh of November, aged eighty-five. The town had been shelled to rubble in the war and was still rebuilding around him; why he was there at all, the accessible record does not say. He had outlived the general staff he mocked, the ministry that lent him out, the cylinder the Americans copied, and every officer who stood at Nantes and watched him read the army's cipher without its key. David Kahn, writing the standard account of him a generation later, weighed him in a sentence.
stops.quote: the great pragmatist of cryptology. His theoretical contributions are negligible, but he was one of the greatest natural cryptanalysts the science has seen.
stops.quote_source: David Kahn, The Codebreakers (rev. ed., Scribner, 1996), 244, quoted with page citation in the en.wikipedia article 'Étienne Bazeries'
suggested_refs: Rosario Candela, The Military Cipher of Commandant Bazeries (New York: Cardanus Press, 1938), the principal English technical monograph on his cipher

stops.name: Noyon, the grave that is not in the record
stops.date_confidence: the date is an ordering device only, standing for the days after the death; no burial record exists in any source reached. fr.wikipedia, en.wikipedia, bibmath, and cryptiana all mention no tomb, grave, or cemetery, and the Léonore notice returned only a search header. This stop states a gap rather than a fact
stops.campa: No cemetery register, no headstone, no family vault has been located for him. The Légion d'honneur file records the death and stops there. The encyclopaedias record the death and stop there. The cryptologic literature, which knows the exact pages on which he printed his key phrases, does not know where his body is. A municipal or genealogical search at Noyon might settle it in an afternoon; nobody in this research could make that search, and so it stands as a hole rather than a guess.
suggested_refs: Municipal and cemetery registers of Noyon, Oise, November 1931, not consulted in this research
sources: Absence recorded after fetching fr.wikipedia, en.wikipedia, bibmath.net, and cryptiana.web.fc2.com, none of which mention a burial

stops.name: Port-Vendres, the name on the war memorial
stops.date_confidence: the inscription is attested through fr.wikipedia's citation of the monumentsmorts.univ-lille.fr database, consulted 19 October 2019; the date of the plaque's erection is recorded nowhere reached, and the ISO date here is only that consultation date, used to place the stop at the end of the file. The database has since moved to monuments-aux-morts.fr and the primary listing could not be reloaded
stops.campa: Port-Vendres puts his name on the monument aux morts, the one place in France where he is physically commemorated. The inscription gives the town, the date of birth, the cylinder, and then the claim about the German codes of the first war that no archive has ever itemised. It is the town's memory of him rather than the archive's: a fishing port keeping the record of a boy who left it in 1863 and who appears, in every source that survives, never to have come back.
stops.quote: Commandant Etienne BAZERIES / cryptanalyste militaire français / né à Port-Vendres le 21 août 1846 / inventeur du cylindre de BAZERIES / reconnu pour avoir cassé les codes / allemands pendant la première / guerre mondiale.
stops.quote_source: Commemorative plaque, monument aux morts, Port-Vendres, as reproduced in the fr.wikipedia article 'Étienne Bazeries', citing monumentsmorts.univ-lille.fr (consulted 19 October 2019)
suggested_refs: The monuments-aux-morts database record for Port-Vendres, Pyrénées-Orientales
